Bayesian phylogenetic model of the trait gradient, with latent beta

Source: R/trait_gradient_brms.R
trait_gradient_brms.Rd

Fits with brms a bivariate phylogenetic mixed model in which the position of each species along the gradient (\(\beta\)) and its mean trait (\(\bar t\)) are latent species effects, estimated from every site of the species, and returns the phylogenetic signal of \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and \(\bar t\) with their credible intervals. Unlike trait_gradient_phylo(), which first computes \(\beta\) and then models it with a standard error, here the uncertainty of \(\beta\) enters the model directly.

Usage

trait_gradient_brms(
  x,
  tree,
  ou_alpha = NULL,
  prior = NULL,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = floor(iter/2),
  cores = 1,
  seed = NA,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

Result of trait_gradient().

tree

Phylogeny (phylo) with branch lengths; species not in it are left out.

ou_alpha

NULL for Brownian motion, or the strength \(a\) of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, in units of 1 / branch length.

prior

Priors as a brmsprior object (from brms::prior()), on the standardised scale, or NULL for the defaults in Details.

chains, iter, warmup, cores, seed

Passed to brms::brm().

...

Further arguments to brms::brm(), such as backend = "cmdstanr"; control defaults to list(adapt_delta = 0.95).

Value

An object of class mc_trait_gradient_brms, a list with

signal

the phylogenetic share \(\lambda\) of \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and the mean, and the phylogenetic correlations of \(\beta\) with the mean and with \(\alpha\): estimate (posterior median), lower, upper (95% interval).

variances

the phylogenetic and species variances of the three quantities, in squared trait units.

species

posterior median and 95% interval of \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and the mean of each species.

diagnostics

largest R-hat, smallest bulk and tail effective sample sizes, number of divergent transitions, and ok.

fit

the brmsfit.

data, center, scale

the data of the model and the standardisation.

Details

Each population (species \(i\) in site \(j\)) contributes two observations: the mean of its site, \(p_{ij}\) (without the focal species, as chosen in trait_gradient()), and its trait value \(t_{ij}\). The model is $$p_{ij} = \mu_p + u^p_i + v^p_i + e^p_{ij}, \qquad t_{ij} = \mu_t + u^t_i + v^t_i + e^t_{ij},$$ where \((u^p, u^t)\) are phylogenetic effects with covariance \(\Sigma_u \otimes A\) (\(A\) the phylogenetic correlation matrix under Brownian motion), \((v^p, v^t)\) are species effects without phylogeny with covariance \(\Sigma_v \otimes I\), and the residuals are independent. So \(\beta_i = \mu_p + u^p_i + v^p_i\), \(\bar t_i = \mu_t + u^t_i + v^t_i\) and \(\alpha_i = \bar t_i - \beta_i\), computed for each draw of the posterior.

With ou_alpha, \(A\) is the correlation matrix of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with strength \(a\) = ou_alpha and a fixed root, as in trait_gradient_phylo(): \(C_{ij} = e^{-a(d_i + d_j - 2 s_{ij})} (1 - e^{-2 a s_{ij}}) / (2a)\), scaled to correlations. \(a\) is taken as known, not estimated: take it from the OU fit of trait_gradient_phylo() for \(\beta\) (response == "beta", model == "OU", column a), which is in the same units. The same \(a\) applies to \(\beta\) and \(\bar t\), because their phylogenetic correlation needs one matrix. As \(a\) goes to 0 the matrix is that of Brownian motion; at large \(a\) it approaches the identity, and the phylogenetic and species effects can no longer be told apart (the function warns). Comparing values of \(a\) by cross-validation needs one response at a time, brms::loo(fit, resp = "sitemean"), because the two responses are fitted to different subsets of rows; the comparison is then conditional on the other response.

The phylogenetic share of the variance among species is \(\lambda = \sigma^2_u / (\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_v)\), between 0 (no phylogenetic signal) and 1 (the structure of A only: Brownian motion, or the OU process given). On a tree that is not ultrametric, scaling the Brownian covariance to correlations is not Brownian motion, because the tips have different variances. For \(\alpha\), \(\sigma^2_u(\alpha) = \sigma^2_u(t) + \sigma^2_u(p) - 2 \rho_u \sigma_u(t) \sigma_u(p)\), and likewise for \(\sigma^2_v(\alpha)\). The phylogenetic correlation of \(\beta\) with \(\bar t\) is \(\rho_u\), and with \(\alpha\) it follows from the same terms.

Both responses are centred on the mean trait value and divided by its standard deviation, so that \(\alpha\) keeps its meaning, and the results are returned in trait units. Weights (from species_weights in trait_gradient()) are divided by their mean, so that they change the relative influence of populations without changing their number. brms treats a weighted observation as that many full observations, so unequal weights, such as abundances, make the posterior too narrow: the effective sample is \((\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2\) rather than the number of populations. The function warns when this is below 70% of the populations; species_weights = "occurrence" avoids the problem.

Priors, on the standardised scale: normal(0, 1) for the intercepts, exponential(1) for the standard deviations of species effects and residuals, and lkj(2) for the correlations; give prior to change them. Two independent exponential(1) priors on the phylogenetic and species standard deviations put a U-shaped prior on \(\lambda\): a quarter of its mass below 0.1 and a quarter above 0.9. With few species the posterior of \(\lambda\) follows that prior. Check convergence (diagnostics: R-hat below 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes above 400, no divergent transitions, over the population-level, group-level and species effects, lp__ and the two \(\lambda\)) and the fit, with bayesplot::pp_check() on the result, before reading the estimates.

Limits

The phylogenetic part is Brownian motion or an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a given strength, shared by both responses; trait_gradient_phylo() estimates the strength. Site means of species that share a site are almost the same number, but the model treats them as independent observations, so the posterior of \(\beta\) is somewhat too narrow when species share many sites. The site mean of a population also contains the trait values of the species it lives with, so when relatives co-occur, the phylogenetic correlation \(\rho_u\) of \(\beta\) and \(\bar t\) is inflated by their shared values, not only by niche conservatism. The residuals of the two responses are taken as independent (no residual correlation), which ignores the slope of the trait on the gradient within species; trait_gradient() estimates those slopes. Sites where a species is the only species have no site mean without it and enter only its trait; a species that is alone in all its sites has no data on \(\beta\), and its \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) are returned as NA.

Splitting the variance among species into a phylogenetic and a non-phylogenetic part needs many species. In trials with 18 species the posterior of \(\lambda\) had modes near 0 and 1 and the chains did not mix (R-hat 1.04–1.27), even with adapt_delta = 0.99 and tighter priors. In 20 trials with 39–45 species, 30 sites and the default settings (4 chains of 2000 iterations), niches that evolved by Brownian motion gave \(\lambda_\beta\) near 1 (median 0.998–0.9995) in 8 of 10 trials, 5 of them passing every diagnostic; niches without phylogenetic signal gave \(\lambda_\beta\) near 0 (median 0.001–0.005) in 8 of 10 trials, but none passed every diagnostic (bulk ESS 180–400, and up to 4 divergent transitions). In the remaining 4 trials the chains split between the two ends (R-hat 1.39–1.75). With 4000 iterations and occurrence weights for species, the chains mixed (R-hat at most 1.03) but most fits had divergent transitions: all 10 without phylogenetic signal (2–298 of 8000 draws), where \(\lambda_\beta\) was again near 0 (median 0.008–0.04). Intermediate signal is not recovered. In 20 trials where the niches followed Pagel's \(\lambda = 0.5\), the posterior median of \(\lambda_\beta\) ranged from 0.007 to 0.81 (median across trials 0.04): the 95% interval contained 0.5 in 12 and excluded 0 in only 3, and only 4 fits passed every diagnostic. With about 40 species the model tells strong signal from none, but it pulls intermediate signal toward 0, and a \(\lambda_\beta\) near 0 is no evidence that \(\beta\) lacks phylogenetic structure. Use trait_gradient_phylo() to test the signal, and do not read a fit that fails diagnostics.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # interactive() && requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("treeshapesim", quietly = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(20)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(15), species_traits(tree, lambda = 1),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 100,
                              seed_steps = 1:5)
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 5, local_adaptation = 0.5, intraspecific_sd = 1)
tg <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance")
bayes <- trait_gradient_brms(tg, tree, chains = 4, cores = 4)
bayes$diagnostics
bayes$signal
bayesplot::pp_check(bayes, resp = "sitemean")
}
